title: THE MAN GOD STRUCK DEAD AFTER HE BETRAYED HIS BROTHER’S WIDOW
paragraphs: THE MAN GOD STRUCK DEAD AFTER HE BETRAYED HIS BROTHER’S WIDOW
He thought nobody would see what he was doing in secret. But Genesis 38 reveals a terrifying truth about selfishness, broken promises, and the God who refuses to abandon the vulnerable.
“And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also.” — Genesis 38:10 (KJV)
There is a man in the Bible who died because of something he did when nobody else was watching.
No battlefield. No sword. No public confrontation.
Just a man, a woman who had already buried her husband, and a decision made in the privacy of their marriage bed.
His name was Onan.

And if you have ever used someone while pretending to love them, made a promise you never intended to keep, taken what you wanted while withholding what another person desperately needed, or convinced yourself that your secret actions do not matter because nobody can see them...
You need to stay with this story.
Because the most frightening part of Genesis 38 is not simply that a man died.
It is what his actions revealed about his heart.
And the most beautiful part is that, centuries later, Jesus Christ would enter the world through the very family whose shame this chapter exposes.
A family marked by betrayal became part of the bloodline through which the Savior came.
That is not an excuse for sin.
That is the astonishing power of grace.
But before we reach the grace, we must walk through the scandal.
And this one is uncomfortable.
Judah, one of the sons of Jacob, had three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah.
His firstborn, Er, married a woman named Tamar.
Scripture tells us that Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death (Genesis 38:7).
We are not told exactly what Er did.
The Bible does not give us permission to invent his crimes.
It simply tells us that God saw his wickedness.
And Tamar became a widow.
Imagine that for a moment.
A woman enters marriage expecting a future. A home. Children. Someone with whom to grow old.
Then suddenly she is standing in the shadow of death.
Her husband is gone.
Her future is uncertain.
And in the ancient world, where a woman's social and economic security could depend heavily upon her family relationships and children, widowhood could leave her painfully vulnerable.
Tamar was not merely grieving a husband.
She was facing the possibility of losing her place in the family and the future she had been promised.
Then Judah spoke to his second son.
“Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother.” — Genesis 38:8 (KJV)
To modern ears, that command may sound strange.
But it belonged to an ancient family obligation later described in the law of Moses in Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
When a man died without a child, his brother could be called upon to marry the widow so that the deceased brother's family line and inheritance would not disappear.
The first son born from that union would carry on the dead brother's name in the legal and family sense.
The Hebrew verb used in Genesis 38:8 is וְיַבֵּם (wəyabbēm), from the root יבם (y-b-m), referring to performing the duty of a husband's brother.
This was not simply a command to produce a baby.
It involved family responsibility, protection of a widow, and preservation of a deceased brother's household.
Genesis 38 takes place before the Mosaic law was given, so we should not pretend that Judah was quoting Deuteronomy. But the passage reflects the same kind of family duty later regulated there.
Onan knew what was expected.
And he knew what he wanted.
Those two things were not the same.
Genesis 38:9 tells us:
“And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother.” (KJV)
Read that carefully.
Onan did not simply refuse the arrangement openly.
He entered the relationship while deliberately preventing the outcome that was central to the obligation he had accepted.
He took the sexual privileges of the union while withholding the family responsibility attached to them.
The Hebrew expression וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה (wəšiḥēt ʾarṣāh) describes his action of spilling or wasting his semen on the ground.
And the final clause explains his intention:
לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו
Ləviltī nətān-zeraʿ ləʾāḥîw.
“So as not to give offspring to his brother.”
That last phrase matters enormously.
The text does not leave us guessing about his motive.
He deliberately refused to provide offspring for his deceased brother.
He wanted the relationship without fulfilling the responsibility.
He wanted the benefit without bearing the cost.
And Tamar was the one left waiting.
Again.
There is something deeply disturbing about that.
Because selfishness does not always announce itself with cruelty.
Sometimes it arrives wearing the appearance of cooperation.
Sometimes it says, “I am here for you,” while quietly arranging everything around its own advantage.
Sometimes it allows another person to believe a promise is being fulfilled when, behind the scenes, that promise is being deliberately sabotaged.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story still feels painfully modern.
There are people who want loyalty but refuse to be faithful.
People who want forgiveness but refuse to repent.
People who enjoy being loved but never intend to love sacrificially.
People who speak about God in public while exploiting trust in private.
And there are others who have been left carrying the consequences of those choices.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe somebody kept you waiting for a future they never intended to build.
Maybe somebody benefited from your kindness while secretly withholding the truth.
Maybe you trusted a person who knew exactly how much you had already suffered, and they still chose themselves at your expense.
If so, do not miss what happens next.
Tamar's pain was not invisible to God.
Genesis 38:10 says:
“And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also.” (KJV)
The Hebrew is direct:
וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
Wayyēraʿ bəʿênê YHWH ʾăšer ʿāsāh.
Literally, in sense:
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
Notice that the passage does not say Onan was punished merely because he did not father a child.
It connects God's judgment with what Onan did, and the preceding verse specifically identifies his deliberate refusal to provide offspring for his brother.
This distinction is important.
Genesis 38:8–10 has sometimes been used as though it were a complete biblical teaching about contraception or every sexual act that does not result in conception.
But that goes beyond what the passage explicitly establishes.

Christians have different theological positions concerning contraception, and those discussions require examining broader biblical teachings about marriage, sexuality, children, and the purposes of sexual intimacy.
The immediate concern in Genesis 38 is Onan's deliberate betrayal of his family obligation, in a situation involving a vulnerable widow and his deceased brother's line.
The narrative presents his behavior as evil before God.
It does not provide a comprehensive explanation of every moral question concerning reproduction.
And it certainly does not authorize us to declare that people who experience infertility, miscarriage, childlessness, or reproductive difficulties are being punished by God.
That would be a cruel misuse of Scripture.
Jesus Himself rejected the assumption that every tragedy can be traced to a particular personal sin (John 9:1–3).
Onan's death was a specific divine judgment reported in a particular biblical narrative.
It is not a formula by which we can explain the suffering or death of people today.
But the moral seriousness remains.
God sees what people deliberately hide.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that nothing in creation is hidden from His sight.
The God who sees public worship also sees private motives.
The God who hears our prayers also hears the promises we never intended to honor.
The God who knows our generosity also knows when we use someone else's vulnerability for our own advantage.
And that should sober every one of us.
Not because every hidden failure will be met with the same immediate judgment Onan experienced.
Scripture does not teach that.
But because no hidden sin is hidden from the Lord.
There is a difference between appearing righteous and actually walking in righteousness.
There is a difference between religious language and a surrendered heart.
And there is a difference between feeling sorry that something has been exposed and genuinely repenting of the wrong.
But here is where the story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Onan dies.
Yet Tamar's suffering does not end.
Judah tells her to remain a widow in her father's house until his youngest son, Shelah, grows up.
But Genesis 38:11 reveals that Judah was afraid Shelah might die like his brothers.
Tamar was sent away to wait.
And wait.
And wait.
Eventually Shelah grew up.
But Judah did not give him to Tamar as promised.
The man responsible for protecting her future withheld it.
And this is where the story begins to expose more than one man's sin.
Onan was guilty.
But Judah was not innocent.
The father who condemned the behavior of his sons would soon be confronted with his own unrighteousness.
And that is a warning to anyone who finds it easier to recognize sin in somebody else than to confront it within themselves.
It is possible to speak strongly about holiness while hiding from the truth about our own conduct.
It is possible to demand accountability from others while making excuses for ourselves.
It is possible to look respectable in the eyes of people and still have something deeply wrong before God.
Later in Genesis 38, Tamar, having been denied the promised marriage, disguised herself and encountered Judah, who did not recognize her.
He solicited her for sex, and she conceived.

The chapter does not present deception or sexual wrongdoing as God's ideal. It describes a deeply broken family situation in which Judah's failure of responsibility had left Tamar without the future he had promised.
When Judah learned that Tamar was pregnant, he called for her to be brought out and burned.
Imagine the hypocrisy.
The man who had participated in the encounter was ready to condemn the woman involved.
He knew his own actions.
But he did not yet know that she possessed the evidence.
Tamar produced Judah's signet, cord, and staff—the items he had left as a pledge.
And suddenly, the man who had pronounced judgment was forced to face himself.
Then came one of the most powerful admissions in Genesis.
“She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son.” — Genesis 38:26 (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase is:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Ṣādqāh mimmennī.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Judah was not declaring that every action Tamar took was morally perfect.
He was acknowledging that, in their conflict, she had a more just claim than he did, because he had failed to fulfill his obligation.
For a moment, the excuses stopped.
The hypocrisy was exposed.
The man who had been ready to condemn another person had to confess his own wrongdoing.
And that may be the moment some of us need more than anything.
Not another explanation.
Not another excuse.
Not another carefully constructed version of the story that makes us look innocent.
Just the courage to say:
I was wrong.
I hurt someone.
I broke my word.
I chose myself.
I need God's mercy.
Because repentance begins when we stop defending what God is calling us to surrender.
And yet, as astonishing as all this is, the greatest revelation is still coming.
Tamar gave birth to twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez's name would become part of a genealogy that leads through generations of broken, complicated, imperfect human beings.
To David.
And ultimately...
To Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:3 records Judah as the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
And Matthew's genealogy eventually reaches Jesus, who is called the Christ.
Think about what that means.
God did not erase Tamar from the story.
He did not conceal her name because her circumstances were scandalous.
He did not pretend Judah's family had been righteous all along.
The Gospel of Matthew places this deeply troubled family history in the ancestry of the Messiah.
Not because God approved of every action in that family.
Not because evil somehow became good.
But because human sin could not overturn God's redemptive purpose.
The scandal was real. But the scandal was not the final word.
And here is the breathtaking difference between Onan's selfishness and Christ's love.
Onan was unwilling to fulfill a costly responsibility for the sake of another.
Jesus willingly gave Himself for people who could never earn His sacrifice.
Onan sought his own benefit while withholding what was owed.
Jesus, though He was rich, became poor for our sake, as 2 Corinthians 8:9 teaches.
Onan's story reveals a man protecting himself at another person's expense.
Jesus reveals the Savior who laid down His life for others.
Philippians 2:5–8 tells us that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
And Mark 10:45 declares that the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Do you see the contrast?
One man chose selfishness when love demanded responsibility.
The Savior chose sacrifice when love demanded everything.
And the beauty of the Gospel is not merely that Jesus shows us how to become better people.
It is that Jesus came to save sinners.
People like Judah.
People who have betrayed trust.
People who have been hypocritical.
People who have concealed shame.
People who have spent years justifying the very things that wounded others.
People like us.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after we had proven ourselves worthy.
Not after our past had become respectable.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Because the cross tells the truth about sin while revealing the depth of God's mercy.
Sin is serious enough that Christ had to die for our redemption.
Grace is powerful enough that those who turn to Him in faith can be forgiven and made new.
And perhaps you have reached this part of the story carrying something you have never told anyone.
Something you did.
Something you allowed.
A relationship you damaged.
A promise you broke.
A season of selfishness that still haunts you.
Or perhaps you are the person who was wounded.
The one who waited.
The one who trusted.
The one who was used.
The one who watched someone walk away without ever acknowledging what they had done.
Listen carefully.
God's mercy does not require you to pretend that what happened was acceptable.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
And restoration does not always mean returning to an unsafe relationship or trusting an unrepentant person again.
But in Jesus Christ, the past does not have to remain the master of your future.
The guilty can repent.
The wounded can seek healing.
The proud can be humbled.
The ashamed can come into the light.
And the broken can find grace.
Not because every consequence disappears.
Not because every relationship is restored.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem people who surrender themselves to Him.
First John 1:9 gives us this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
There is no promise here that we can continue deliberately in sin and claim grace as permission.
Romans 6:1–2 rejects that thinking.
True grace calls us out of the darkness.
It teaches us to deny ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
It leads us toward honesty, humility, restitution where possible, changed behavior, and a life increasingly shaped by Christ.
So let me ask you something deeply personal.
Are you living like Onan, taking what you want while withholding what love and righteousness require?
Are you living like Judah, condemning in others what you refuse to confront in yourself?
Or are you living like Tamar, carrying the pain of promises broken by people who were supposed to protect you?
These are not identical experiences.
But each one brings us to the same urgent question.
What will you do when God's Word confronts your heart?
You can close this article.
You can tell yourself it is about someone else.
Or you can bring the truth before Jesus.
Without pretending.
Without hiding.
Without negotiating.
Perhaps your prayer tonight needs to be simple.

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have done, what I have suffered, and what I have hidden. Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken in me. Give me the courage to repent, to make right what I can, and to walk in Your truth. I cannot rewrite my past, but I surrender my life to You. Make me new. Amen.”
And if that prayer speaks to where you are, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to expose private details or relive trauma in a comment section. A few sincere words are enough to invite encouragement and prayer.

And if you have personally experienced the mercy of Christ, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and God has not finished working in the lives of broken people.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with shocking Bible stories and leave them unchanged.
Not to replace the local church, faithful pastors, or the personal study of Scripture.
But to help bring people back to the Word of God, to the truth of the Gospel, and to a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
Every article we publish, every biblical reflection we share, and every resource we make available is intended to serve that mission.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God's blessing can be purchased.
You glorify God first and foremost through faith in Jesus Christ and a life of obedience to Him.
But one way believers can honor the Lord is by voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work, according to their ability and conviction.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
You are choosing to stand alongside a mission that seeks to bring Scripture, conviction, encouragement, and Christ-centered discipleship into the daily lives of readers.
These products are not the reason to support the Gospel.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Not merely to increase views.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be someone who has been quietly living under shame, justifying hidden sin, or carrying the wounds of betrayal.
Someone who needs to hear that God sees what is done in secret.
Someone who needs the courage to repent.
Someone who needs to know that the Gospel offers forgiveness without denying the seriousness of sin.
Someone who has almost given up believing that a broken life can still be redeemed.
Because discipleship is not built on one emotional moment.
It is a daily walk of learning to trust and obey Jesus.
And before you leave, remember how this story began.
A man refused to give his deceased brother an heir.
A widow was left without the future she had been promised.
A father hid behind his own hypocrisy.
A family became entangled in scandal.
Yet from that family line, generations later, came Jesus Christ—the Savior who did not withhold Himself from sinners, but willingly gave His life for their redemption.
That is the Gospel's extraordinary announcement.
Not that human beings are better than their stories suggest.
But that God's mercy is greater than repentant sinners deserve.
Not that wrongdoing is harmless.
But that the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
Not that scandal should be celebrated.
But that scandal does not have to be the final chapter of a redeemed life.
So do not walk away from Genesis 38 merely remembering the man who died.
Remember the widow whose story God did not erase.
Remember the father who was forced to acknowledge his sin.
Remember the family whose shame could not stop God's redemptive plan.
And above all...
Remember Jesus.
The One who came into a world of broken promises and kept every promise the Father gave Him.
The One who entered humanity's darkness and remained without sin.
The One who carried our guilt to the cross.
The One who rose again.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life through faith in His name.
Onan's story reminds us that God sees what we hide. The cross reminds us that Jesus can redeem what we finally surrender.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth of all is this:
The family tree carried the scandal, but the Savior who came through it carried the cross.
